# Comparisons

"Large", "expensive" and "fast" mean nothing alone: compared with what? A value with nothing next to it is a claim with no ground. To show two things side by side is one of the best ways to make a person look closely, and the step from one thing to two is the large one: it starts curiosity and analysis. Two beetles tell much more about beetles than one beetle.

## Give each value a thing to compare with

- **A number gets a reference**: the same value a month ago, the mean, the plan, the value of the neighbor. Choose the reference that the question needs, and name it.
- **A second view of the same thing** shows what one view hides. From one angle a crowd stands behind a player; from the other, most of them are far away.
- **Side by side, or one over the other.** Two things of the same type can stand next to each other, or lie on each other at the same scale, thus the difference is seen directly.
- **A unit repeated for each thing, with one design**, is the strongest form of this; see [Repeated elements](./small-multiples.md).
- **More than two things let the person learn a rule.** From five examples of finished work, a person sees what stays the same and what is free, with no written standard. But also in a set, people pick two and compare those.

## Compare with a thing that the person knows

Very large, very small and very far things cannot be imagined. Put them at a scale of the person's own life.

- **Lay the unknown thing over a known one, at the same scale**: a lake over a country, an airport next to its city, a comet over a town, a continent on a planet.
- **A height is harder to imagine than a length.** A three-floor house drawn behind a jump gives the height at once. A walk that the person has done (the length of a known street or district) gives a depth or a height better than a tower does.
- **Choose a reference that most of the audience has seen**, and prefer one with the same direction: a long ship next to a long thing, not next to a tall one. A surprising reference draws attention, which is a use of its own, but it explains less.
- **Still give the numbers.** A picture of a jump with a house behind it lacks the height in meters. The reference gives the sense; the number gives the fact.

## Compare the things themselves

- **Where you can, show the real things, not an abstraction of them**: their size, shape and color, not bars of their areas. It is more exact and far more interesting to look at.
- **For an abstract quantity, find a form in which the picture is the data.** The share of advertisements in a newspaper: the pages themselves, with the advertisements marked. Nobody can doubt that.
- **A beautiful form is permitted when it is honest about what it compares.** Mountains drawn as a landscape compare only their heights (the shapes are not to scale), where plain marks at the heights would do. The picture makes people want to look, and that has a value; say what is to scale and what is not.

## A comparison can lie better than a chart

A comparison is so clear that it is believed at once, and nobody checks it. Thus it is the perfect way to mislead, also by accident.

- **Compare the same quantity that the picture shows.** Five ships drawn in a row for "five times the mass" are read as five times the length. A picture of a size must compare sizes; for mass, money or a count, use a chart with an axis.
- **The same scale and the same distortion for the two things.** Areas on a map differ by the projection: a country far from the equator looks much too large. A comparison of two countries is honest only when the two are drawn at the same latitude or in a projection that keeps areas.
- **Build the comparison so that it cannot be doubted.** A map laid over itself, turned by a half turn around the equator, puts north and south land side by side with the same distortion at each place. Prefer such a form to one that asks for trust.
- **A picture that cannot be checked (a tower built from all phones ever sold) is an illustration.** Say where the numbers come from.
- **A set of things at "true size" must be to one scale.** If one thing in a row of countries is plainly too large against its neighbor, the whole picture is not believed.

## Finding the difference in things that are nearly the same

When the purpose is to find what differs (two configurations of a product, two plans, two versions), do not show the two as they are.

- **Mark the differences**, and let the common part recede. Two columns of ten equal lines and one that differs make the person do the search.
- **Say the common part one time**, above the two, and list only what differs, with what the difference costs.
- **The form of the list**: when each difference has a value on the two sides ("1 bank account" against "2"), a small table with a column for each thing and only the rows that differ. When one thing only adds to the other, a plain list of what it adds. The column of the thing that the person has now shows their own state, not the general text.
- **Keep the equal lines only when the list of features is itself a purpose of the screen**; then mark the lines that differ.
- **Before and after**: the same view, the same scale, the same frame, and a color for what changed (the ice that is gone drawn as water).

## What to draw

- A value with its reference next to it, named.
- An unknown size laid over a known one at one scale, with the numbers.
- The real things side by side where that is possible.
- Marked differences between things that are nearly the same.
